newsitem.title: IRAQ: Iraq oil-for-food observers in place in March, U.N..
newsitem.headline: Iraq oil-for-food observers in place in March, U.N..

text.p: International observers to supervise an oil-for-food deal with Iraq are due in place by mid-March but food distribution is not likely to start until April, U.N. sources in Baghdad said on Wednesday.

They said it would be at least mid-April before food stocks piled up in sufficient quantities to be handed out to Iraqis suffering under United Nations sanctions imposed after the 1990 invasion of Kuwait.
The sources said about half of the 222 U.N. monitors were already in Iraq and the rest were expected in Baghdad in the next 10 days.
One U.N. source said both the United Nations and the Iraqi side had agreed to embark on immediate distribution once supplies reach Iraq.
"We do not have to wait for all items in the ration card to arrive to commence our work. If there is enough wheat flour we will distriubte it. Better to have something than nothing," the source said.

He said he hoped Iraq's more than 20 million people would have enough wheat flour and rice by April. For other items, like vegetables, sugar, tea and detergents, the Iraqis will have to wait, he added.
A shipment of 25,000 tonnes of wheat is scheduled to arrive at Iraq's southern port of Umm Qasr by end of March.
"It is expected that late March and April will see a steady flow of humanitarian supplies to the country," another source said.
Iraq has repeatedly complained to the United Nations about delay in the arrival of humanitarian supplies. It started partial oil exports worth $2 billion every six months in December last year.
The U.N. offered the partial sales deal to alleviate the suffering of the Iraqi people.
The observers are to ensure that food and medicine bought from the oil sales are fairly distributed throughout the country.

Trade Minister Mohammed Mehdi Saleh said on Monday the U.N. had only approved nine of the 222 contracts submitted to it since December. He said out of the more than 100 contracts on medicine only one had been approved.

U.N. sources said the observers were free to move around Iraq and during the past few days had made inspection tours of flour mills, food agents, silos and major ration centres in and outside Baghdad.
